dots-1.title: Where 30 worlds settle: people, wealth, families
dots-1.caption: One dot per world: its mean over iterations 500 to 1,499, divided by the mean of that value over the 30 worlds, so that every statistic is on the same scale and 1 is the average world. The bar is the median. A column of dots close to 1 means the worlds settle alike; a tall column, that they do not. The dots are spread sideways only so they do not hide one another.
dots-1.recipe:
**Runs.** The 30 baseline runs `B1-100000-s001` … `B1-100000-s030`: the baseline B1 at 100,000 tokens, seeds 1 to 30, 1,500 iterations each (every setting is listed in Chapter 9). They are made with `python3 gol_lab.py run E10`.

**Data.** From each run's `GraphOfLifeRuns/<run>/stats.jsonl`, which holds one row per recorded phase: `phase` 1 is the world just after reproduction, `phase` 2 just after the game, and every statistic is a field of the row (see [What a run records](../notes/frames-and-stats.md)).

1. For each run and statistic, average the statistic over the rows with 500 ≤ `iteration` ≤ 1,499 (rows with `phase` 1 for births, 2 for the rest; `a/b` means the row's `a` divided by its `b`).
2. Divide each run's average by the mean of the 30 averages.
3. Plot one dot per run, with a bar at the median.

**To make it again:** `python3 book_figures.py seed`.

memory.title: How long a world remembers its level
memory.caption: For each statistic, the correlation between a world's level in one stretch of 100 iterations and its level a given number of iterations later, over all pairs of stretches in the 30 worlds. 1 would mean a world stays exactly where it was; 0 that where it was says nothing about where it will be. Because each world's own mean is taken away first, a world cut into only 14 stretches shows negative correlations at long lags even if it simply wandered: the grey dashes are what a random walk, cut and centred the same way, gives (averaged over 200 sets of as many walks), and the grey dots what levels with no memory at all give.
memory.recipe:
**Runs.** The 30 baseline runs `B1-100000-s001` … `B1-100000-s030`: the baseline B1 at 100,000 tokens, seeds 1 to 30, 1,500 iterations each (every setting is listed in Chapter 9). They are made with `python3 gol_lab.py run E10`.

**Data.** From each run's `GraphOfLifeRuns/<run>/stats.jsonl`, which holds one row per recorded phase: `phase` 1 is the world just after reproduction, `phase` 2 just after the game, and every statistic is a field of the row (see [What a run records](../notes/frames-and-stats.md)).

1. For each run, cut iterations 100 to 1,499 into 14 stretches of 100 and take the mean of the statistic in each.
2. Subtract from each run's 14 values their own mean, so that only the run's movement remains.
3. For a lag of L stretches, pair every stretch with the one L later, in every run, and take the Pearson correlation of all the pairs together.
4. References: 30 series of 1,400 steps, each step normal with mean 0 — summed (a random walk) or not (no memory) — cut, centred and correlated the same way; the mean over 200 such sets (generator seeded with 13).

**To make it again:** `python3 book_figures.py seed`.

between.title: Variation between worlds, and within each world
between.caption: All the variation of a statistic's 100-iteration levels — 14 stretches in each of 30 worlds — split into the part that lies between the worlds' own averages (blue) and the part that is each world moving around its own average (the rest of the column, grey).
between.recipe:
**Runs.** The 30 baseline runs `B1-100000-s001` … `B1-100000-s030`: the baseline B1 at 100,000 tokens, seeds 1 to 30, 1,500 iterations each (every setting is listed in Chapter 9). They are made with `python3 gol_lab.py run E10`.

**Data.** From each run's `GraphOfLifeRuns/<run>/stats.jsonl`, which holds one row per recorded phase: `phase` 1 is the world just after reproduction, `phase` 2 just after the game, and every statistic is a field of the row (see [What a run records](../notes/frames-and-stats.md)).

1. Take each run's 14 stretch means as for the figure above.
2. Between: the variance (n − 1 in the denominator) of the 30 runs' own averages.
3. Within: the mean over runs of the variance of each run's 14 values.
4. Draw between ÷ (between + within).

**To make it again:** `python3 book_figures.py seed`.

halves.title: First half against second half
halves.caption: One dot per world. Left: its mean number of agents over iterations 100–749 (x) against its mean over iterations 750–1,499 (y). Right: the same for connections. A dot on the dashed diagonal had the same mean in both halves. r is the correlation over the 30 dots.
halves.recipe:
**Runs.** The 30 baseline runs `B1-100000-s001` … `B1-100000-s030`: the baseline B1 at 100,000 tokens, seeds 1 to 30, 1,500 iterations each (every setting is listed in Chapter 9). They are made with `python3 gol_lab.py run E10`.

**Data.** From each run's `GraphOfLifeRuns/<run>/stats.jsonl`, which holds one row per recorded phase: `phase` 1 is the world just after reproduction, `phase` 2 just after the game, and every statistic is a field of the row (see [What a run records](../notes/frames-and-stats.md)).

1. For `nodes` and `edges`, average over the rows with `phase` = 2 and 100 ≤ `iteration` ≤ 749, and over 750 ≤ `iteration` ≤ 1,499.
2. Plot the second against the first, one dot per run; r is their Pearson correlation ([correlation](../notes/correlation.md)).

**To make it again:** `python3 book_figures.py seed`.

stretch.title: Longer looks, smaller differences
stretch.caption: For each statistic, how much the 30 worlds differ — the standard deviation of their averages divided by the mean — when each world is measured by its average over its last L iterations, for L from 100 to 1,400.
stretch.recipe:
**Runs.** The 30 baseline runs `B1-100000-s001` … `B1-100000-s030`: the baseline B1 at 100,000 tokens, seeds 1 to 30, 1,500 iterations each (every setting is listed in Chapter 9). They are made with `python3 gol_lab.py run E10`.

**Data.** From each run's `GraphOfLifeRuns/<run>/stats.jsonl`, which holds one row per recorded phase: `phase` 1 is the world just after reproduction, `phase` 2 just after the game, and every statistic is a field of the row (see [What a run records](../notes/frames-and-stats.md)).

1. For each length L, average the statistic over the rows with 1,500 − L ≤ `iteration` ≤ 1,499 in each run.
2. Divide the standard deviation of the 30 averages (n − 1 in the denominator) by their mean.

**To make it again:** `python3 book_figures.py seed`.

seeds-needed.title: Seeds a condition needs
seeds-needed.caption: How many worlds each of two conditions needs for a change of a given size in the average to be found four times in five at the 5% level, if worlds vary as much as these do. Dashed: worlds measured over their last fifth (iterations 1,200–1,499); solid: over iterations 500–1,499. The grey line is 30 seeds.
seeds-needed.recipe:
**Runs.** The 30 baseline runs `B1-100000-s001` … `B1-100000-s030`: the baseline B1 at 100,000 tokens, seeds 1 to 30, 1,500 iterations each (every setting is listed in Chapter 9). They are made with `python3 gol_lab.py run E10`.

**Data.** From each run's `GraphOfLifeRuns/<run>/stats.jsonl`, which holds one row per recorded phase: `phase` 1 is the world just after reproduction, `phase` 2 just after the game, and every statistic is a field of the row (see [What a run records](../notes/frames-and-stats.md)).

1. Measure each run by its average over the stretch, and compute the spread c = sd ÷ mean of the 30 averages.
2. For a change Δ (as a share of the mean), n = 2 (z₁ + z₂)² c² / Δ², with z₁ = 1.960 (5%, two-sided) and z₂ = 0.842 (power 80%); round up.

**To make it again:** `python3 book_figures.py seed`.
